danish.title: Sjette bog (1808–10) — Kapitel 24
paragraphs: Der fandt ingen forlovelsesceremoni sted, og Natáshas forlovelse med Bolkonskij blev ikke offentliggjort; fyrst Andrej insisterede på det. Han sagde, at da det var ham, der bar ansvaret for udsættelsen, burde han bære hele byrden; at han havde givet sit ord og bundet sig for evigt, men at han ikke ønskede at binde Natásha og gav hende fuldkommen frihed. Hvis hun efter seks måneder følte, at hun ikke elskede ham, ville hun have fuld ret til at afvise ham. Naturligvis ønskede hverken Natásha eller hendes forældre at høre om dette, men fyrst Andrej stod fast. Han kom hver dag til familien Rostov, men opførte sig ikke over for Natásha som en forlovet; han sagde ikke »du« til hende, men brugte det formelle tiltaleord, og han kyssede kun hendes hånd. Efter forlovelsen opstod der ganske andre, intime og naturlige forhold mellem dem. Det var, som om de ikke havde kendt hinanden indtil da. Begge kunne godt lide at huske, hvordan de havde betragtet hinanden, da de endnu intet var for hinanden; de følte sig nu som helt andre mennesker: dengang var de kunstige, nu naturlige og oprigtige. I begyndelsen følte familien en vis tvungenhed i samværet med fyrst Andrej; han virkede som et menneske fra en anden verden, og i lang tid trådte Natásha familien til at vænne sig til ham, idet hun stolt forsikrede dem alle, at han kun så anderledes ud, men i virkeligheden var ligesom dem alle, og at hun ikke var bange for ham, og det burde ingen andre heller være. Efter få dage vænnede de sig til ham og førte uden tvang deres sædvanlige liv i hans nærhed, og han deltog deri. Han kunne tale om landbrug med greven, om mode med grevinden og Natásha, og om albums og håndarbejde med Sonja. Undertiden udtrykte husholdet, både indbyrdes og i hans nærhed, deres forundring over, hvordan det hele var sket, og over de tydelige tegn, der havde forudsagt det: fyrst Andrejs komme til Otrádnoe og deres ankomst til Petersborg, og ligheden mellem Natásha og fyrst Andrej, som hendes barnepige havde bemærket ved hans første besøg, og Andrejs møde med Nikolaj i 1805 og mange andre hændelser, der tydede på, at det måtte ske.

I huset herskede den poetiske kedsomhed og stilhed, der altid ledsager tilstedeværelsen af et forlovet par. Ofte, når alle sad sammen, holdt alle mund. Undertiden rejste de andre sig og gik ud, og parret, der blev alene tilbage, forblev stadig tavse. De talte sjældent om deres fremtidige liv. Fyrst Andrej var bange og skammede sig ved at tale om det. Natásha delte dette som alt andet, hans følelser, som hun bestandig anede. En gang begyndte hun at spørge ham om hans søn. Fyrst Andrej rødmede, som han ofte gjorde nu — det syntes Natásha særlig godt om ved ham — og sagde, at hans søn ikke ville bo hos dem.
»Hvorfor ikke?« spurgte Natásha med forskrækket stemme.
»Jeg kan ikke tage ham fra hans bedstefar, og desuden...«
»Hvor ville jeg have elsket ham!« sagde Natásha, der straks gættede hans tanke. »Men jeg ved, at du ønsker at undgå ethvert påskud til at finde fejl ved os.«

Undertiden kom den gamle greve hen, kyssede fyrst Andrej og spurgte ham om råd angående Petjas uddannelse eller Nikolajs tjeneste. Den gamle grevinde sukkede, når hun så på dem; Sonja var altid bange for at være i vejen og forsøgte at finde undskyldninger for at lade dem alene, selv når de ikke ønskede det. Når fyrst Andrej talte (han kunne fortælle meget godt), lyttede Natásha til ham med stolthed; når hun talte, lagde hun med frygt og glæde mærke til, at han så opmærksomt og prøvende på hende. I rådvildhed spurgte hun sig selv: »Hvad leder han efter i mig? Han forsøger at opdage noget ved at se på mig! Hvad nu, hvis det, han søger i mig, ikke er der?« Undertiden faldt hun i et af de gale, muntre lunder, der var så karakteristiske for hende, og da elskede hun især at høre og se, hvordan fyrst Andrej lo. Han lo sjældent, men når han gjorde det, hengav han sig helt til sin latter, og efter et sådant latterudbrud følte hun sig altid ham nærmere. Natásha ville have været fuldkommen lykkelig, hvis ikke tanken om den forestående adskillelse, der nærmede sig, havde skræmt hende, ligesom den blotte tanke om den fik ham til at blegne og fryse.

Aftenen før hans afrejse fra Petersborg bragte fyrst Andrej Pierre med, som ikke havde været hos familien Rostov en eneste gang siden ballet. Pierre virkede forvirret og forlegen. Han talte med grevinden, og Natásha satte sig ved et lille skakbord med Sonja og indbød derved fyrst Andrej til også at komme. Det gjorde han.
»De har kendt Bezukhov (Pierre) længe?« spurgte han. »Holder De af ham?«
»Ja, han er sød, men meget distræt.«
Og som sædvanligt, når hun talte om Pierre, begyndte hun at fortælle anekdoter om hans distraktion, hvoraf nogle endda var opdigtet om ham.

»Ved du, jeg har betroet ham vores hemmelighed? Jeg har kendt ham fra barnsben. Han har et hjerte af guld. Jeg beder dig, Natalie,« sagde fyrst Andrej med pludselig alvor. »Jeg rejser, og himlen ved, hvad der kan ske. Du kan ophøre med at... ja, jeg ved, jeg ikke skal sige det. Blot dette: hvad end der sker med dig, når jeg ikke er her...«
»Hvad kan der ske?«

»Hvilke sorger end måtte komme,« fortsatte fyrst Andrej, »beder jeg Dem, frøken Sophie, uanset hvad der sker, om udelukkende at henvende Dem til ham for råd og hjælp! Han er den mest distræte og mærkelige fyr, men han har et hjerte af guld.«

Hverken hendes far, hendes mor, Sonja eller fyrst Andrej selv havde kunnet forudse, hvordan adskillelsen fra hendes elskede ville virke på Natásha. Rød i ansigtet og ophidset gik hun hele den dag rundt i huset med tørre øjne og var optaget af de mest ligegyldige ting, som om hun ikke forstod, hvad der ventede hende. Hun græd ikke engang, da han til afsked kyssede hendes hånd for sidste gang. »Rejs ikke!« sagde hun i en tone, der fik ham til at spekulere på, om han virkelig ikke burde blive, og som han længe huskede bagefter. Hun græd heller ikke, da han var rejst; men i flere dage sad hun på sit værelse med tørre øjne og interesserede sig ikke for noget og sagde blot nu og da: »Åh, hvorfor rejste han?«

Men fjorten dage efter hans afrejse kom hun sig til omgivelsernes overraskelse pludselig af sin sjælelige sygdom, lige så hurtigt som den var kommet, og blev igen sig selv, men med en forandring i sit moralske udtryk, ligesom et barn rejser sig efter en lang sygdom med et ændret ansigt.

english.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 24
paragraphs: There was no formal betrothal ceremony, and Natasha's engagement to Bolkonsky was not announced; Prince Andrew insisted on this. He said that since he was responsible for the delay, he alone should bear the burden of it; that he had given his word and was bound forever, but that he didn't wish to bind Natasha and was giving her complete freedom. If after six months she felt she didn't love him, she would have every right to reject him. Naturally neither Natasha nor her parents wanted to hear of this, but Prince Andrew was firm. He came to the Rostovs' every day, but didn't behave toward Natasha as an engaged man: he didn't use the intimate "thou" but addressed her as "you," and kissed only her hand. After the engagement, completely different relations sprang up between them — intimate, natural, and sincere. It was as if they hadn't known each other before. Both loved to recall how they had thought of each other when they were still nothing to one another; they felt themselves now to be entirely different people — then they had been artificial, now they were natural and genuine. At first the family felt somewhat constrained around Prince Andrew; he seemed like a man from another world. For a long time Natasha had to train the family to get used to him, proudly assuring them all that he only seemed different but was really just like everyone else, and that she wasn't afraid of him and nobody else should be either. After a few days they grew accustomed to him and went on with their usual way of life in his presence, and he took part in it. He could talk about estate management with the count, about fashion with the countess and Natasha, and about albums and needlework with Sonya. Sometimes the household, both among themselves and in his presence, marveled at how it had all come about and at the obvious signs that had foretold it: Prince Andrew's visit to Otradnoe, their coming to Petersburg, the resemblance between Natasha and Prince Andrew that the old nurse had noticed on his first visit, and Andrew's encounter with Nicholas in 1805, and many other incidents that seemed to prove it was all meant to be.

In the house that poetic stillness and quiet reigned which always accompanies the presence of an engaged couple. Often when they were all sitting together everyone would fall silent. Sometimes the others would get up and leave, and the couple, left alone, would still remain silent. They rarely spoke of their future life. Prince Andrew was afraid and ashamed to bring it up. Natasha shared this feeling, as she did all his feelings, which she constantly intuited. Once she began asking about his son. Prince Andrew blushed, as he often did now — Natasha especially loved this in him — and said that his son would not live with them.
"Why not?" asked Natasha, alarmed.
"I can't take him away from his grandfather, and besides..."
"How I would have loved him!" said Natasha, instantly guessing his thought. "But I understand — you want to avoid giving anyone a reason to criticize us."

Sometimes the old count would come over, kiss Prince Andrew, and ask his advice about Petya's education or Nicholas's career. The old countess would sigh as she looked at them; Sonya kept getting nervous that she was in the way and tried to find excuses to leave them alone, even when they didn't want her to. When Prince Andrew spoke — and he could tell a story very well — Natasha listened with pride; when she spoke, she noticed with a mixture of fear and joy that he watched her attentively and searchingly. She asked herself in bewilderment: "What is he looking for in me? He's trying to find something by studying me! What if what he seeks isn't there?" Sometimes she fell into one of the wild, giddy moods that were so characteristic of her, and then she particularly loved to watch how Prince Andrew laughed. He laughed rarely, but when he did, he gave himself over to it completely, and after such laughter she always felt closer to him. Natasha would have been perfectly happy if the thought of the approaching separation had not terrified her, just as the mere thought of it made him turn pale and cold.

On the eve of his departure from Petersburg, Prince Andrew brought Pierre along. Pierre had not been to the Rostovs' once since the ball. He seemed distracted and embarrassed. He was talking to the countess, and Natasha sat down at a little chess table with Sonya, silently inviting Prince Andrew to come too. He did so.
"You've known Bezukhov a long time?" he asked. "Do you like him?"
"Yes, he's a dear, but very funny."
And as usual when talking about Pierre, she began telling stories of his absent-mindedness, some of which had even been made up about him.

"Do you know, I've told him our secret? I've known him since childhood. He has a heart of gold. I beg you, Natalie," Prince Andrew said with sudden seriousness, "I'm going away, and heaven knows what may happen. You may stop loving... All right, I know I'm not supposed to say that. Just this, then: whatever may happen to you when I'm not here..."
"What could happen?"

"Whatever trouble may come," Prince Andrew continued, "I beg you, Mademoiselle Sophie, whatever happens, turn to him alone for advice and help! He's the most absent-minded and absurd fellow, but he has a heart of gold."

Neither her father, nor her mother, nor Sonya, nor Prince Andrew himself could have predicted how the separation from her fiance would affect Natasha. Flushed and agitated, she went about the house all that day, dry-eyed, busying herself with the most trivial matters as if she didn't understand what was coming. She didn't even cry when, saying goodbye, he kissed her hand for the last time. "Don't go!" she said in a tone that made him wonder whether he really ought not to stay — and which he remembered long afterward. Nor did she cry when he was gone; but for several days she sat in her room, dry-eyed, taking no interest in anything, only saying now and then: "Oh, why did he go away?"

But two weeks after his departure, to the surprise of everyone around her, she recovered from her emotional illness just as suddenly, and became her old self again — though with a change in her inner character, as a child gets up after a long illness with a different expression on its face.
